Severity is left at high and its re-rating on this corrected premise is Scot's call, not auto-applied. Verification standard recorded in the AWS BAA correction: re-attestation of the operative condition requires both that the credential env vars are present on the serving revision and that sts:GetCallerIdentity under that credential returns the BAA'd account.

findings.title: Word-prediction cache holds the raw pre-scrubber user utterance in a process-global structure outside the PiiScrubber boundary, and is not tenant-scoped

remediation.options: PRIMARY ISSUE, unscrubbed retention outside the redaction boundary. The cache key is built from the raw sentence BEFORE PiiScrubber runs (lib/ai_word_predictor.rb:47), and entries live in a process-global CACHE constant. CACHE_TTL (1800s / 30 minutes) is checked only when deciding whether to reuse an entry on lookup (lib/ai_word_predictor.rb:48-51); expired entries are not deleted until capacity eviction (CACHE_MAX=500) or overwrite. On a low-traffic process with fewer than 500 distinct keys, a raw utterance can therefore remain in heap memory for the process lifetime, so describing this as 30-minute retention understates the heap-dump exposure. Verbatim, unredacted AAC utterance content, which is exactly what the compliance corpus says is redacted before it is handled, sits in process memory outside that control. It is reachable by a heap dump, a debug endpoint, or any exception reporter that captures locals or constants. Every compliance document that cites PiiScrubber as THE control on user-authored content is inaccurate for as long as this is true. SECONDARY ISSUE, tenant scoping. CACHE has no user, organization, or district discriminator, so two users in different districts who compose the byte-identical sentence share an entry. This is the weaker of the two arguments and should not be led with: the second user already possesses the input they typed, so what they gain is the model's output for their own sentence, not another learner's content. It still contradicts the mandatory district data-isolation requirement and should be fixed. FIX. Key on a hash of the SCRUBBED sentence rather than the raw one, so no verbatim utterance is retained; include a tenant discriminator (organization or user id) in the key; and either delete on TTL expiry or stop claiming a 30-minute retention bound. Then decide explicitly whether a cache shared across tenants is wanted at all for user-composed content.

closureEvidence.verifierNote: Verified 2026-08-29 against origin/staging 8afabd1d2. Both halves remediated in lib/ai_word_predictor.rb. (a) Pre-scrubber content no longer keys the cache: the sentence passes through PiiScrubber.redact_for_ai first and only the scrubbed form reaches cache_key_for (lines 92-103). (b) The key is tenant-scoped and no longer raw: cache_key_for SHA-256 digests [cache_scope(user), locale, scrubbed sentence, time_of_day, topic] joined on a NUL separator, and cache_scope resolves to the organization, falling back to the user id, so one tenant's entry cannot serve another's. Concurrency and unbounded growth were addressed in the same work: CACHE is guarded by CACHE_MUTEX and expired entries are swept on store.
closureEvidence.attestation: Scot Wahlquist 2026-08-29: attested verified-closed during the open-High triage sweep; accepted the recorded code/live-state trace at origin/staging 8afabd1d2 as the verification basis.

disposition.rationale: CEO triage 2026-08-29. Closed as fixed. Raw utterance no longer reaches the cache key and the key is tenant-scoped.

findings.notes: Found by adversary review of PR 725; rationale reordered 2026-08-02 after the same reviewer noted the original write-up led with the weaker cross-tenant argument. Activation and TTL wording corrected 2026-08-03 after Codex review of this PR. PREMISE CORRECTED 2026-08-04: the note previously read 'Currently unexercised while Bedrock is unconfigured: resolve_api_config returns nil and predict returns early at lib/ai_word_predictor.rb:34-35, so nothing reaches the cache write.' That is no longer the operative history. Revision 00013-76w mounted the Bedrock credentials at 2026-08-03T08:23:02Z, and a live AiWordPredictor.predict call completed successfully at 2026-08-04T05:44:42Z, so the cache write at line 135 DID execute in production with a key built from the raw pre-scrubber sentence. The utterance in that single call was an internal verification string containing no user or student data, so no real user content was retained; the defect is nonetheless now demonstrated in production rather than theoretical. Credentials were withdrawn at 2026-08-04T06:31:46Z (revision 00014-5rw), returning the path to unexercised. This finding should be scheduled on its stated fix (hash of the SCRUBBED sentence plus a tenant discriminator) rather than deferred behind an 'unexercised' label, since any future credential mount re-activates it immediately. Once credentials are mounted and resolve_api_config succeeds, the cache write at line 135 runs even when the model call fails -- the rescue at lines 90-94 returns [] and execution still stores CACHE[cache_key] = { words: words, ts: Time.now }. Activation condition is AiClient.configured? (credential pair present), not a successful Bedrock completion; same mount trigger as LL-1b0d78dbe6. Severity HIGH on the unscrubbed-retention argument alone; the reviewer's initial medium was revised up after weighing the mandatory district-isolation rule and for consistency with LL-1b0d78dbe6. Severity remains Scot's call.

findings.title: Masquerade shows no on-screen indication of whose account is being operated

remediation.options: Cheapest path (template only, no server change): render the already-stashed operator identity beside the existing Stop Masquerading controls. session.original_user_name is set at masquerade start (app/frontend/app/components/masquerade.js:61, app/frontend/app/controllers/organization.js:48), restored at app/frontend/app/services/session.js:510, and already read by the isMasquerading computed at app/frontend/app/controllers/application.js:52,56 with a stash fallback at :62. Option 2, only if the server must be authoritative: serialize the acting operator via lib/json_api. Scope of @true_user (set at app/controllers/application_controller.rb:182,196): the private_logging checks in app/controllers/api/logs_controller.rb, the PaperTrail whodunnit at :185/:199, and the authorization plus audit-attribution actor in app/controllers/concerns/api/schema_explorer.rb:90,103 and app/controllers/concerns/api/system_settings_access.rb:7. It never reaches lib/json_api. PR #714 (staging, 2026-07-30) added persistent Stop Masquerading controls (app/frontend/app/components/app-navbar-authenticated-inner.hbs:64,183,211; app/frontend/app/templates/application.hbs:928,1276,1304), which signal THAT a masquerade is active but not WHOSE record is open.

findings.notes: Raised manually 2026-08-04 from a working session, not from an /audit-run fan-out. Severity and disposition are Scot's to set. Accountability scope, corrected after dual review: PaperTrail records user:<operator>:as:<target> (app/controllers/application_controller.rb:185,199) ONLY on the models and attributes it versions, namely the Board (app/models/board.rb:64) and User (app/models/user.rb:44) attribute allowlists, and destroy-only on LogSession (app/models/log_session.rb:28). UserGoal carries no has_paper_trail at all. Surviving versions are pruned by User.flush_old_versions (app/models/user.rb:3646). So a masquerading admin's create or update of a student's log session or goal is NOT distinguishable after the fact. This finding covers the UI indicator gap only; the absence of any masquerade AuditEvent is a separate issue and is not yet filed. 2026-08-05: owned by Melissa; Option 1 UI fix on branch fix/melissa-masquerade-operator-indicator (show session.original_user_name beside Stop Masquerading). Status remains open pending Scot disposition after merge.

findings.title: Masquerade produces no AuditEvent; the site-admin branch impersonates any user with no disclosure record

remediation.options: Write an AuditEvent at masquerade authorization in both branches of application_controller.rb (site-admin at :181, org-manager at :188-205), recording the acting operator, the target user, and the branch that authorized it. Prior art already exists in this codebase and should be generalized rather than reinvented: app/controllers/concerns/api/schema_explorer.rb:102-104 defines audit_user_key as (@true_user || @api_user)&.global_id precisely so a disclosure is booked to the admin who performed the read rather than the account being viewed as. That treatment covers one endpoint and nothing else. Note masquerade has no session concept to hook: it is a per-request as_user_id param or X-As-User-Id header (:177), so the event must be emitted on the authorization path, and de-duplicated per operator/target rather than per request. The org-manager branch already caches its authorization decision in Redis for 30 minutes (:195), which is a natural de-dup window; the site-admin branch has no cache and no gate at all.

closureEvidence.verifierNote: Verified 2026-08-29 against origin/staging 8afabd1d2. app/controllers/application_controller.rb:177-210 calls record_masquerade_audit! on BOTH masquerade branches (branch "site_admin" and branch "org_manager"). The fix exceeds what the finding asked for: a non-:ok return from the audit write refuses the masquerade with api_error 503 "Audit log write failed; masquerade refused", so there is no path that masquerades without an AuditEvent rather than merely one that logs after the fact. Present in the deployed production image (3 occurrences in `git show 73a8f6339`).
closureEvidence.attestation: Scot Wahlquist 2026-08-29: attested verified-closed during the open-High triage sweep; accepted the recorded code/live-state trace at origin/staging 8afabd1d2 as the verification basis.

disposition.rationale: CEO triage 2026-08-29. Closed as fixed. Masquerade is now audit-gated and fail-closed on both branches.

findings.notes: Promoted from PR #742 review (adversary) on 2026-08-04. Surfaced by the Claude adversary pass during dual review of PR #742, and verified against code at that PR's base: grep for AuditEvent in app/controllers/application_controller.rb returns zero occurrences. FERPA accounting-of-disclosures and HIPAA 164.312(b) audit controls therefore have no record that an admin viewed or acted inside a given student account. The site-admin branch grants impersonation of ANY user on Organization.admin.manager? alone, with no consent record. This is the accountability half of the masquerade problem; LL-cde54765c6 covers the separate UI indicator gap and explicitly does not claim to cover this. Related: PaperTrail does not close the gap either, since log_session.rb:28 versions on destroy only, user_goal.rb has no has_paper_trail, and User.flush_old_versions (user.rb:3646) prunes surviving versions.

findings.title: SubscriptionMailer#new_subscription sends a user's IP address to iplocate.io with no user-type or consent gate, to a third party absent from the subprocessor register (GDPR Art. 28/44, COPPA)

remediation.options: Found by the 2026-08-08 quarterly subprocessor review (the cycle that fell due 2026-07-20 and was not performed). SubscriptionMailer#new_subscription reads the user's stored device IP (@user.devices[0].settings['ip_address']) and GETs https://iplocate.io/api/lookup/<ip> whenever ENV['IPLOCATE_API_KEY'] is set, on any new subscription. TWO distinct defects. (1) UNGATED: unlike the sibling call in lib/external_tracker.rb:23, which is gated on external_email_allowed? && supporter_registration? && !cookies_opted_out?, this call site has NO user-type check and NO consent gate, so it can fire for any account type including a child or student account. An IP address is personal data under GDPR and is COPPA-relevant for an under-13 user. (2) UNDISCLOSED: iplocate.io is named nowhere in docs/legal/SUBPROCESSORS.md, so this is an Article 28 register omission of the same class as the three flows recorded on 2026-07-21 and the Speech-to-Text flow recorded on 2026-07-22 (LL-1eb9a2435b). Options: (a) gate this call site to match external_tracker.rb, or drop geolocation from the notification email entirely, since the recipient is an internal admin address (NEW_REGISTRATION_EMAIL) rather than the user; (b) add an iplocate.io subprocessor row with DPA status and a data-flow description; (c) confirm whether a DPA exists with iplocate.io at all. NOT YET ESTABLISHED and needed before triage: whether this path can fire for a child/student account in practice, and whether it has ever fired in production. Stripe is a SEPARATE omission found by the same review and is not part of this finding.

findings.title: Hard delete leaves LogSnapshot records undeleted (GDPR right-to-erasure)

remediation.options: LogSnapshot rows are keyed by user_id (app/models/log_snapshot.rb:11) and are created through api/snapshots_controller.rb#create. Neither Flusher.flush_user_content nor flush_user_completely references LogSnapshot, user.rb declares no dependent: :destroy for it, log_session.rb declares no has_many, and db/schema.rb declares no foreign keys at all, so nothing cascades at any level. A hard delete therefore leaves log_snapshots rows carrying a supervisor-supplied name, a date range, a device_id and a location_id, keyed to a deleted user. Fix: add a LogSnapshot.where(user_id:) sweep to flush_user_content alongside the ButtonSound / UserVideo sweeps added in PR #721, with regression coverage. Note the retained location_id already dangles, because ClusterLocation is swept at lib/flusher.rb:19. Scoped to LogSnapshot only: UserExtra and ContactMessage are named in the same unverified set in the retention draft but were not traced, and no claim is made about them.

disposition.rationale: Confirmed real Article 17 / FERPA erasure defect by manual trace. Set at medium rather than the high carried by LL-854b1d3853: that finding retained a child's actual voice and video content, whereas a LogSnapshot retains only a saved report window (label, date range, device_id, location_id) and its location_id already dangles because ClusterLocation is erased. Accepted; fix by adding the Flusher sweep. Production exposure is NOT established: api/snapshots_controller.rb is a live API path, and static inspection cannot determine whether production rows exist. No claim is made either way.

findings.notes: Surfaced 2026-08-10 while verifying the PR #721 Path A successor drafts against code, per the /re-attest-record 'verify the doc is true now' gate. Distinct from LL-854b1d3853, which covers UserVideo and off-board ButtonSound only. Severity and disposition approved by Scot on 2026-08-10 after a recommendation from the Codex reviewer; the agent proposed the row and did not decide it.

findings.title: Client-supplied context.topic reaches Bedrock unscrubbed and is absent from the AiApiLog egress record

remediation.options: Run PiiScrubber.redact_for_ai over ctx[:topic] in AiWordPredictor.predict (alongside the sentence scrub at lib/ai_word_predictor.rb:92) and pass only the scrubbed value into normalize_context/system_prompt. Merge the topic's scrub_result[:findings] into the pii_findings and pii_detected passed to log_ai_call (lib/ai_word_predictor.rb:155-168), and include the scrubbed topic in request_summary so the AiApiLog row reflects the full egress payload. Alternatively constrain topic to a server-side enum/board-id reference rather than free text.

closureEvidence.verifierNote: Verified 2026-08-29 against origin/staging 8afabd1d2. The egress half is remediated: scrub_context (lib/ai_word_predictor.rb:206-214) runs ctx[:topic] through PiiScrubber.redact_for_ai and returns the scrubbed topic; it is called at line 98 BEFORE the cache key is built, and its pii_found and findings are merged into the pii_detected and pii_findings passed to log_ai_call (lines 99-100, 155-168), so a topic-borne detection is recorded on the AiApiLog row rather than dropped. RESIDUAL, tracked separately as LL-c259638711 (open Low, added 2026-08-30 from Codex review of PR #887): request_summary is still built from the scrubbed sentence alone and omits the scrubbed topic, so the log line does not show which topic accompanied the call. That is a log-completeness gap on already-scrubbed content, not an egress gap.
closureEvidence.attestation: Scot Wahlquist 2026-08-29: attested verified-closed during the open-High triage sweep; accepted the recorded code/live-state trace at origin/staging 8afabd1d2 as the verification basis.

findings.notes: Surfaced by privacy finder on 2026-08-12. Tier 1 runtime AI path. Only `sentence` is scrubbed (lib/ai_word_predictor.rb:92); `topic` is interpolated verbatim into the Bedrock system prompt. Reachable via POST /api/v1/word_suggestions (config/routes.rb:196), which affirmatively permits the field (app/controllers/api/word_suggestions_controller.rb:61, ctx.permit(:time_of_day, :topic)). Blast radius is bounded because the destination is the BAA'd Bedrock route and no first-party client currently populates context.topic (app/frontend/app/utils/ai_word_predictor.js:131 posts only sentence/locale/count), but the frontend's analogous topic_context is board name (app/frontend/app/controllers/board/index.js:181), a free-text field AAC users routinely personalize with caregiver/clinician names. Distinct from LL-16ef84ad9a, which concerns the cache key, not prompt egress. Independent secondary defect: AiApiLog pii_detected/pii_findings/request_summary understate what actually left the system. | adversary: confirmed -- Traced full path: only sentence hits PiiScrubber.redact_for_ai (lib/ai_word_predictor.rb:92); ctx flows raw through normalize_context into system_prompt's topic interpolation at line 340 with no scrub. word_suggestions_controller.rb:61 permits :topic. AiApiLog request_summary only records the scrubbed sentence, so pii_detected understates actual egress.

disposition.rationale: CEO triage 2026-08-29. Closed as fixed on the egress claim, which is what made this a High: the context topic is scrubbed before it leaves the process and its detections reach the audit row. The request_summary omission is carried forward as open Low LL-c259638711 rather than holding a High row open.

findings.title: PredictionEntry rows survive account deletion, retaining per-user AAC vocabulary sequences indefinitely

remediation.options: Add PredictionEntry.where(user_id: user.id).each { |e| Flusher.flush_record(e) } to Flusher.flush_user_content (lib/flusher.rb:363-416), following the LogSnapshot precedent added for LL-1e2ab28aab. Optionally also declare has_many :prediction_entries, dependent: :destroy on User, but note db/schema.rb defines no add_foreign_key entries at all, so Flusher is the only reliable erasure path.

findings.notes: Surfaced by privacy finder on 2026-08-12. prediction_entries (db/schema.rb:519-530) is keyed by user_id (null: false) and stores prefix/next_word pairs, i.e. the user's actual communication vocabulary and word-sequence patterns. Neither User (app/models/user.rb:16-23) nor Flusher.flush_user_content references it, and the schema has zero foreign keys, so there is no cascade. Same erasure-gap class as LL-854b1d3853 and LL-1e2ab28aab, different table; no existing (ruleKey, file) match in the register. Rows are written by PredictionEntry.sync_for_user via POST /api/v1/prediction_entries/sync. | adversary: confirmed -- Repo-wide grep for PredictionEntry/prediction_entr finds no lib/flusher.rb hit; flush_user_content enumerates many models but not this one. Schema has no FK/cascade and User has no has_many :prediction_entries.

findings.title: PredictionEntry stores AAC vocabulary content in plaintext columns without secure_serialize

remediation.options: Move prefix/next_word/score/source into a single serialized column protected by secure_serialize (per app/models/concerns/secure_serialize.rb), matching Utterance, LogSession, and UserExtra. If the per-column btree indexes (idx_prediction_entries_unique, idx_prediction_entries_prefix) make that impractical for lookup performance, record an explicit accepted-risk rationale in the register rather than leaving the divergence undocumented.

findings.notes: Surfaced by privacy finder on 2026-08-12. Every peer model holding user-generated AAC content encrypts it: Utterance (app/models/utterance.rb:18), LogSession (app/models/log_session.rb:29), UserExtra (app/models/user_extra.rb:8). PredictionEntry does not, despite prefix/next_word being derived directly from a communicator's button selections. Confidence is medium because this is a divergence from codebase convention and CLAUDE.md's secure_serialize guidance rather than a breach of an explicit written control; the indexing requirement is a legitimate competing constraint that Scot may accept. | adversary: confirmed -- No secure_serialize or encrypts in the 63-line model; schema shows plain indexed string columns. Noted tension: prefix/next_word carry lookup indexes used by for_prefix, so column encryption is not a drop-in fix.

findings.title: focus_generated_words_usage writes caller-supplied words into any AiFocusWordSet with no ownership or tenant check

remediation.options: Scope the lookup to the caller's tenant before mutating: compare focus_set.seed_organization_global_id against @api_user.managing_organization&.global_id (or seed_user_global_id against @api_user.global_id) and return 404 on mismatch. Alternatively stop accumulating applied_words on the shared row and record usage in a per-user/per-org join record, keeping the shared row limited to the AI-generated output it already caches.

findings.notes: Surfaced by privacy finder on 2026-08-12. AiFocusWordSet rows are global, keyed only by prompt_hash (db/schema.rb:115, unique index), and record_usage! (app/models/ai_focus_word_set.rb:111-122) appends caller-supplied final_words into applied_words and flips status. Any holder of a valid API token can therefore write their own applied vocabulary into a row attributed via seed_user_global_id / seed_organization_global_id to a different district. Breaks the mandatory district data-isolation requirement in CLAUDE.md. Disclosure risk is limited because focus_words_response (app/controllers/api/integrations_controller.rb:214-225) serves only words/title/library_id/ai_generated and never applied_words; this is primarily a cross-tenant write/co-mingling defect. | adversary: confirmed -- focus_generated_words_usage checks only the ai_board_generation flag, then find_by_global_id + record_usage! with no org/seed_user comparison. spec/controllers/api/integrations_controller_spec.rb:596-614 itself demonstrates an arbitrary token_user writing into a set it never created.

findings.title: AiFocusWordSet retains seed_user_global_id and prompt text after the seeding user's account is erased

remediation.options: In Flusher.flush_user_content (lib/flusher.rb:363-416), null out seed_user_global_id (and seed_organization_global_id where the org link is the deleted user's only tie) on AiFocusWordSet rows matching the erased user's global_id, mirroring the License nulling already done at lib/flusher.rb:412-415. The generated word list itself may be retained as a de-identified cache entry once the identifiers are severed.

findings.notes: Surfaced by privacy finder on 2026-08-12. ai_focus_word_sets (db/schema.rb:88-118) carries seed_user_global_id, seed_organization_global_id, and free-text scrubbed_prompt/normalized_prompt/title. Flusher's erasure path handles AiApiLog by user_global_id (lib/flusher.rb:29) but has no equivalent for this table, and there is no scheduled cleanup for it anywhere in lib/tasks or render.yaml. The prompt is post-PiiScrubber, which lowers content sensitivity, but the direct user identifier survives erasure. Related to but distinct from the PredictionEntry gap (different table, different identifier column, identifier-nulling rather than row deletion is the appropriate remedy). | adversary: confirmed -- seed_user_global_id set at line 75, stored plain; no lib/flusher.rb reference to the table. Bonus: the low_value prune scope (lines 24-26) also has zero callers anywhere, so there's no automated aging-out path either.

findings.title: anonymous_logs export job writes each publishing user's username to stdout, bypassing the PII-scrubbing log formatter

remediation.options: Drop user.user_name from the progress line and log the global_id only, or replace the puts with Rails.logger.info so the line at minimum passes through PiiScrubbingFormatter. Apply the same treatment to the surrounding progress puts at app/models/log_session.rb:2077, 2086, 2123, 2133 if this method is to keep emitting progress from a worker context.

findings.notes: Surfaced by privacy finder on 2026-08-12. LogSession.anonymous_logs runs in a Resque worker via Progress.schedule (app/controllers/api/logs_controller.rb:409 and app/models/log_session.rb:2125), not only from an interactive console, and its triggering endpoint is in the require_api_token except-list (app/controllers/api/logs_controller.rb:2), so an unauthenticated caller can initiate it. Raw puts bypasses config.log_formatter entirely (config/environments/production.rb:98-114), and that formatter's own header notes it would not scrub usernames anyway. Under Cloud Run the line lands in Cloud Logging, which associates an identifying username with the fact that the account publishes its AAC logs. Severity held at medium because the sink is HIPAA-scoped and access-controlled, making this a defense-in-depth failure rather than external exposure. The export content itself is separately fine: it is double opt-in (allow_log_reports + allow_log_publishing, app/models/log_session.rb:2112) and pseudonymized via per-record HMAC (app/models/user.rb:1409-1417), and UPLOADS_S3_NO_ACL=1 is set in prod (.github/workflows/deploy-cloudrun.yml:273) so the public-read ACL branch in lib/uploader.rb:341 does not apply. | adversary: confirmed -- Line 2111 is a literal puts with user.user_name; PiiScrubbingFormatter only governs Rails.logger. logs_controller.rb:2 excepts :anonymous_logs from require_api_token. Bonus: the puts fires BEFORE the consent check on the next line, so even non-consenting users' usernames are emitted.

findings.title: Article 50 disclosure server-side backstop is present on only 2 of 5 AI ingresses

remediation.options: Extract the disclosure guard used at app/controllers/api/boards_controller.rb:590-594 and app/controllers/api/integrations_controller.rb:107-111 into a shared ApplicationController helper (e.g. require_article_50_disclosure!) and apply it to word_suggestions#create, words#predict, and eval_sessions#narrate, so enabling the article_50_disclosure flag covers all five ingresses atomically. Add a spec asserting every controller that calls AiWordPredictor/AiBoardGenerator/EvalNarrator invokes the guard, so a sixth ingress cannot ship without it.

closureEvidence.verifierNote: Verified 2026-08-19 at staging tip afdfebee7: all 5 AI ingresses now carry the server-side Article 50(1) backstop -- app/controllers/api/boards_controller.rb:584, app/controllers/api/integrations_controller.rb:104, app/controllers/api/word_suggestions_controller.rb:28, app/controllers/api/words_controller.rb:63, and app/controllers/api/eval_sessions_controller.rb:84 each call require_article_50_disclosure!/article_50_disclosure_missing? (app/controllers/application_controller.rb:409,419). Landed via PR #829 (merge e101628ff5ea7cdc80564edbcdb3520ef0691ddf). The regression spec recommended in remediation.options (spec/controllers/article_50_disclosure_backstop_coverage_spec.rb) also landed in #829, but chatgpt-codex-connector flagged it as file-scoped rather than method-scoped (review comment 3815352166, P2): a second unguarded AI action added to an already-covered controller file would still have passed. Fixed in PR #831 (merge afdfebee7485e8b6ca263f1defb29c2eca8f8f1e), which rewrote the scan with RubyVM::AbstractSyntaxTree to assert the guard call inside each AI-calling method's own source span, with a 3-case regression fixture proving the old failure mode is closed. bundle exec rspec on the coverage spec: 9 examples, 0 failures. AMENDED 2026-08-23 on Scot's direction -- the prior sentence ('article_50_disclosure remains AVAILABLE-only (not in ENABLED_FRONTEND_FEATURES), so this is still latent-until-enabled.') was FALSE as a runtime claim. AVAILABLE-only describes CODE; production enables the flag via the default_enabled_features DB Setting. Verified 2026-08-23 (unattested evidence record): the guard is LIVE and gates 29 of 34 users (docs/legal/2026-08-23_article-50-production-flag-verification.md). Awaiting Scot's verified-closed attestation.

findings.notes: Surfaced by privacy finder on 2026-08-12. Five AI ingresses exist: boards_controller#generate_labels, integrations_controller#focus_generate_words, words_controller#predict, word_suggestions_controller#create, eval_sessions_controller#narrate. Only the first two carry the EuJurisdiction.disclosure_required? / article_50_disclosure_shown? backstop. The COPPA and EU-under-16 consent gates are correctly enforced on all five (they live inside the libs as well as the controllers), so this is a transparency-disclosure gap, not a consent gap. AMENDED 2026-08-23 on Scot's direction -- the prior text here was FALSE and is replaced. It read: 'Currently latent because article_50_disclosure is AVAILABLE-only and not in ENABLED_FRONTEND_FEATURES, making all instances of the guard inert today; the defect is that enabling the flag would produce silent partial enforcement.' Correction: AVAILABLE-only is a statement about CODE. Production overrides the code constant through the default_enabled_features DB Setting and the flag IS ENABLED there. Verified 2026-08-23 by direct read (docs/legal/2026-08-23_article-50-production-flag-verification.md, DOC-6c023a20a0 -- an UNATTESTED evidence record): EuJurisdiction.status is :unknown for 34 of 34 users, disclosure_required? is true for 34 of 34 (fail-safe open: only an authoritative :non_eu suppresses), and 29 of 34 were gated at all five AI ingresses as of 2026-08-23T23:23:41Z (probe lingolinq-migrate-stnwz). The guard is NOT inert. On whether the silent partial enforcement this finding warned about actually OCCURRED: all 64 AiApiLog rows fall between 2026-08-04T05:44:42Z and 2026-08-14T21:13:27Z, entirely BEFORE five-ingress coverage reached PRODUCTION (merged to staging 2026-08-19; live in production 2026-08-21 via release #842), so every logged AI call was served while only 2 of 5 ingresses carried the backstop. 63 of 64 carry article_50_disclosure_shown=true; the single false row is at 2026-08-04T05:44:42Z and is consistent with the internal verification call already recorded in CAPABILITY-LEDGER.json (art50-1-disclosure-modal). No AI traffic since 2026-08-14T21:13:27Z. Two limits on that evidence, carried forward from the cited sources: those 63 rows come from 2 DISTINCT ACCOUNTS, not 63 users (2026-08-17_ai-data-flow-classification.md:129), and AiApiLog can UNDER-RECORD -- ai_api_log.rb:100-102 rescues a failed save and returns an unsaved record, and Flusher.flush_user_logs destroys rows per user on erasure. It is therefore not a complete ledger of egress. Because enabled-since is unrecoverable (Setting carries no version history), the partial-enforcement question cannot be closed definitively; the log shows no pattern of undisclosed calls. Tagged GDPR because the schema's frameworks enum has no EU AI Act value; the governing instrument is EU AI Act Art. 50(1). | adversary: confirmed -- EuJurisdiction/article_50 guard exists only in boards_controller.rb:590-593 and integrations_controller.rb:107-110. Read word_suggestions_controller, words_controller#predict, and eval_sessions_controller#narrate in full; none carries the backstop. | REMEDIATED 2026-08-19: all 5 ingresses guarded (#829, e101628ff) and the coverage spec's file-level scoping gap (Codex review comment 3815352166 on #829) closed with a method-scoped AST rewrite (#831, afdfebee7). Status moved open -> remediated-unverified; closureEvidence populated; attestation left empty for Scot.

findings.title: Committed WIF provisioning script omits the assertion.ref branch lock the deploy pipeline names as a control, and reconciles (overwrites) the live provider on every re-run

remediation.options: Add the ref lock to WIF_CONDITION in phase1-setup.sh so the committed script matches the hardened live provider: append `&& assertion.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && assertion.ref_type == 'branch'`. This matters specifically because the script does NOT skip an existing provider -- it deliberately reconciles it via `gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers update-oidc` (phase1-setup.sh:333-337), so any re-run of Phase 1 silently REMOVES the branch lock from production. Also close the gap the script itself defers at phase1-setup.sh:492-495: map attribute.environment and bind the deploy SA principalSet to .../attribute.environment/production rather than repo-wide, so the GitHub environment approval becomes a token-minting condition rather than a workflow-file convention.

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. deploy-cloudrun.yml states this as gate #3 of four: 'The ref guard + the WIF provider's assertion.ref condition, so no other ref can deploy or even mint a deploy token' (deploy-cloudrun.yml:33-34, repeated at :170-171). Live read-only check (gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe github-provider, pool github-pool, location global) confirms the LIVE provider condition DOES include a ref and ref_type clause pinning the main branch -- so the control exists in production but does not exist in the committed provisioning source, and the source actively reverts it. Note also that the workflow-file if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' guard is not itself a boundary: workflow_dispatch executes the workflow definition from the SELECTED ref, so anyone who can push a branch and dispatch Actions can run a copy with the guard and the environment: production key removed. Live pool name is github-pool / provider github-provider, which does not match a naive read of the script's defaults -- confirm live before acting. | adversary: confirmed -- Live provider's attributeCondition includes the ref/ref_type lock; committed WIF_CONDITION at line 329 does not. Script unconditionally reconciles an existing provider via update-oidc, so a re-run would strip the live lock. | SEVERITY DOWNGRADED high -> medium on 2026-08-30 by Scot Wahlquist (CEO). Status stays open; this is a severity decision, not a closure. Basis, verified live on 2026-08-30 rather than inferred: the PRODUCTION provider is correctly hardened. `gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe github-provider --project=lingolinq-prod --location=global --workload-identity-pool=github-pool` returns attributeCondition = "assertion.repository_owner_id == '249911097' && assertion.repository_id == '1024104500' && assertion.repository == 'lingolinq/LingoLinq-AAC' && assertion.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && assertion.ref_type == 'branch'", i.e. the ref/ref_type lock IS present in prod. So there is no current exposure to downgrade away from. What remains is a latent regression footgun: the COMMITTED script omits the ref lock at phase1-setup.sh:329 and unconditionally reconciles an existing provider via update-oidc, so any re-run of Phase 1 silently STRIPS the live branch lock with no error. That is a real defect worth fixing, but it is conditional on a rare, deliberate operator action against a currently-correct production state, which is medium, not high. NOTE for the record: an earlier triage worksheet justified this downgrade on the different and incorrect ground that residual risk was narrow because 'an attacker needs push access to some branch' -- that phrasing implied prod lacked the ref lock. Prod has it. The rationale recorded here supersedes that reasoning; the conclusion is unchanged.

findings.title: GCP production project has no Data Access audit log configuration, so Secret Manager value reads and Cloud SQL data access produce no audit record

evidence.snippet: - Enable Data Access audit logs on Secret Manager + Cloud SQL for HIPAA evidence.

remediation.options: Set an IAM audit config on the production project enabling DATA_READ (and DATA_WRITE where cheap) for secretmanager.googleapis.com and cloudsql.googleapis.com, at minimum. Without it, secretmanager.versions.access -- the operation that returns a plaintext production secret -- is not logged at all, because Data Access logs are off by default and only Admin Activity logs are always-on. Pair with a log sink to a retention-controlled bucket so the evidence outlives the default Cloud Logging retention, and add the audit config to phase1-setup.sh so it is reproducible rather than a console click.

findings.title: Production Cloud Run service is deployed with public ingress, so the direct run.app URL bypasses the load balancer and its attached Cloud Armor policy

remediation.options: Run the ingress lockdown that already exists in the repo (phase5-frontend-lb.sh step 3, gated behind CONFIRM_INGRESS_LOCKDOWN=1) so the web service only accepts traffic from the load balancer. The coupling documented at phase5-frontend-lb.sh:465-474 and deploy-cloudrun.yml:498-507 must be resolved in the SAME change or every subsequent deploy goes red fail-closed: the candidate health probe runs from a public GitHub runner against the candidate---* tag URL, and Cloud Run ingress restrictions apply to tag URLs too. Move that probe behind the LB (tag-targeted serverless NEG) or into the VPC first. Decide explicitly which flips first.

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. Verified live, read-only. `gcloud run services describe lingolinq-web --region=us-central1` reports the ingress annotation as unrestricted, and the service is deployed --allow-unauthenticated (deploy-cloudrun.yml:496). `gcloud compute backend-services list --global` shows the LB backend has a Cloud Armor security policy attached, and `gcloud compute security-policies describe` shows that policy carries four deny(403) rules plus a throttle rule ahead of the default allow. Net effect: the edge WAF deny rules and the edge rate limit are all reachable-around by requesting the service's own run.app hostname. The deploy workflow never passes --ingress, so the service takes the permissive default on every deploy. Application-layer controls (auth, Rack::Attack) still apply on the bypass path; the edge controls do not. | adversary: confirmed -- Live service shows ingress=all and allUsers bound to run.invoker; confirmed the run.app URL returns HTTP 200 directly, bypassing the Cloud Armor policy attached only to the LB backend.

findings.title: Production Cloud SQL instance has deletion protection disabled and is provisioned without it, while automated deploys apply migrations with no pre-migration backup step

remediation.options: Add --deletion-protection to the gcloud sql instances create call in phase3-data-layer.sh (the flag list at :241-255 ends without it) and enable it on the live instance. Consider also raising retained-backups above the 7-day default given FERPA/HIPAA restoration expectations, and adding an on-demand backup step to deploy-cloudrun.yml immediately before the migration Job -- the pipeline currently runs rake db:migrate against production with no snapshot taken in the same run (deploy-cloudrun.yml:417-457), so PITR is the only recovery path for a bad migration. The cutover runbook already carries this as an unchecked box (scripts/gcp/PHASE5-CUTOVER-RUNBOOK.md:45).

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. Verified live, read-only: `gcloud sql instances describe lingolinq-prod-pg` reports deletion protection disabled, automated backups enabled, PITR enabled, 7 retained backups and 7 days of transaction-log retention, no public IPv4, zonal availability. Deleting the instance also discards its automated backups, so deletion protection is the single control standing between one mis-scoped admin command and total loss of the student/patient dataset. Compounds the companion finding that a human principal holds cloudsql.admin. Zonal (non-HA) availability is a deliberate launch-stage cost choice noted in the script and is not raised separately. | adversary: confirmed -- Live instance reports deletionProtectionEnabled=False; create-flag list has no --deletion-protection. PITR + 7 retained backups exist, so this is recoverability-degrading rather than data-destroying.

findings.title: Production Cloud SQL instance accepts unencrypted connections (ssl mode allows unencrypted) and is provisioned with no SSL enforcement flag

remediation.options: Set the instance SSL mode to encrypted-only (gcloud sql instances patch --ssl-mode=ENCRYPTED_ONLY) and add the equivalent flag to the create call in phase3-data-layer.sh so the posture is reproducible. The app path is unaffected: Cloud Run reaches the instance over the Cloud SQL connector socket, which is encrypted independently of the client sslmode value. What the change closes is every OTHER path -- any client reaching the private IP from inside the VPC (a bastion, a future workload, a hand-run psql) can currently negotiate a plaintext session carrying PHI.

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. Verified live, read-only: `gcloud sql instances describe lingolinq-prod-pg` reports the SSL mode as the permissive setting that allows both unencrypted and encrypted connections, and the provisioning script's create flag list (phase3-data-layer.sh:241-255) contains no SSL flag at all. Distinct from open finding LL-ba0585ab93, which is about client-side sslmode/cert verification in config/database.yml; this one is about server-side enforcement on the instance. Related context: config/database.yml:39 defaults DB_SSLMODE to 'disable' on the GCP socket path, so nothing in the stack requests TLS on that connection either -- the encryption there comes from the connector, not from either endpoint's configuration. | adversary: confirmed -- Live sslMode=ALLOW_UNENCRYPTED_AND_ENCRYPTED, requireSsl=False; no SSL flag in the provisioning script. Partial mitigation: instance is private-IP-only with no authorizedNetworks, so exposure requires an in-VPC foothold.

findings.title: The admin_token cookie that gates the Resque admin console is set without HttpOnly, so any XSS can steal an admin console session

remediation.options: Set the cookie with explicit security attributes, matching what config/initializers/session_store.rb:6-10 already does for the app session cookie: cookies[:admin_token] = { value: admin_token, httponly: true, secure: Rails.env.production?, same_site: :lax, expires: 2.hours.from_now }. Consider also scoping path: '/jobby' so the token is not attached to every request to the app, and shortening the 2-hour Redis TTL for an admin console session.

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. This cookie is the sole credential checked by lib/admin_constraint.rb:3-9, which gates the mounted Resque web UI at /jobby (config/routes.rb:35). That UI exposes queued job arguments and allows retry/kill of background jobs. Secure is effectively applied in production because config.force_ssl (config/environments/production.rb:62) makes ActionDispatch::SSL rewrite Set-Cookie, and SameSite=Lax comes from load_defaults 7.2 -- but neither of those adds HttpOnly, so the token remains readable from JavaScript. Exposure is meaningfully increased by the Content-Security-Policy being report-only with unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval (existing open finding LL-c226391436), which means an injected script would not be blocked. | adversary: confirmed -- Line 250 sets a bare cookie value with no options hash, unlike session_store.rb's app cookie. force_ssl already adds `secure` in production, so the residual gap is specifically httponly and same_site.

findings.title: No server-side password strength policy exists; the only minimum-length check is a 6-character Ember computed property, bypassable by a direct API call

remediation.options: Enforce the password policy at the Rails layer, where the boundary actually is. Add validation in app/models/concerns/passwords.rb#generate_password (or a User validation) rejecting passwords below a documented minimum -- NIST SP 800-63B calls for at least 8 characters -- and apply it on every write path: registration (api/v1/users create), password change (app/models/user.rb:2542), password reset (users_controller#password_reset:949), valet password generation, and the org/subscription-driven set at app/models/concerns/subscription.rb:645. Consider a breached-password check against a k-anonymity list rather than composition rules, per the same NIST guidance. Then raise the client-side hint to match, so the UX and the boundary agree.

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. The User model carries no validates declaration for password (grep of app/models/user.rb returns none), and app/models/concerns/passwords.rb#generate_password (:269-274) pre-hashes and stores whatever it is given with no length or complexity check. app/controllers/api/users_controller.rb:5 exempts :create from require_api_token, so account creation is an unauthenticated POST -- a client that skips the Ember form can set a one-character password on a new account, including accounts that later become supervisors with access to child records. This is exactly the failure mode CLAUDE.md's own P2 preflight rule describes: 'Enforcement lives at the server/API (Rails) layer. Client-side Ember flags are UX polish, never the security boundary.' The 6-character client hint is itself below the current NIST minimum. | adversary: confirmed -- register.js:217 is the only length check anywhere; User model has zero validates declarations; api/v1/users#create is exempt from require_api_token. Rack::Attack throttles the endpoint but that is not a strength policy.

findings.title: Failed authentication attempts produce no AuditEvent and no security log line, so credential-stuffing and password-guessing are undetectable after the fact

remediation.options: Emit a structured record on every authentication outcome, not just the success path. Successful logins already log one line (session_controller.rb:552) but no AuditEvent; failures log nothing at all. Write an AuditEvent (event_type 'login_failed' / 'login_succeeded') or at minimum a tagged Rails.logger line carrying only non-identifying fields -- global_id when the account resolved, a truncated/hashed source-IP bucket, device_key, and the failure reason -- never the submitted username or password. Cover the sibling credential-checking endpoints too: users_controller#resend_parental_consent:831, #submit_parental_consent_email:876, :1150, and the oauth/SAML paths. Then alert on rate and on distribution across accounts.

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. SOC2 CC7.2 and HIPAA 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(C) (log-in monitoring) both expect failed access attempts to be recorded. AuditEvent is used extensively for consent, deletion, admin record reads and password change (existing closed finding LL-747bb0e02d), so the mechanism exists and is simply not wired to the authentication outcome. Note the successful-login log line at session_controller.rb:552 is correctly PII-safe (global_id and JSON key names only) and should be the model for the failure path. Also worth noting for the remediation design: config/environments/production.rb:98-108 documents that the PII-scrubbing log formatter does NOT catch names or usernames, so a failure log must not include the submitted identifier. | adversary: confirmed -- Lines 566/568/572 emit no logger call and no AuditEvent; repo-wide AuditEvent grep has no session_controller.rb hit at all, so even the success path lacks an AuditEvent (only a log line).

findings.title: Brute-force protection on login is per-source-IP only at roughly 400 attempts/minute, with no per-account lockout, backoff, or velocity control

remediation.options: Add an account-keyed control alongside the existing IP-keyed one: a Rack::Attack throttle discriminated on the normalized username for /token, oauth2/token/login and the SAML/consent credential endpoints, plus exponential backoff or a temporary lock after N consecutive failures on one account (a pattern the codebase already uses elsewhere -- see the per-user Redis throttle at users_controller.rb:840-850). Pair it with the failed-auth logging finding so the lock is observable. Separately, verify empirically what Rack::Attack's req.ip resolves to behind the Cloud Run load balancer before tuning any IP-keyed limit.

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. config/initializers/throttling.rb:62-74 keys every throttle on req.ip with a 3-second period, so /token permits 20 attempts per 3 seconds (~400/min) from one address and unlimited attempts from a distributed source, and there is no counter attached to the targeted account at all -- grep for failed_login / lockout / locked_out / login_attempt across app/, lib/ and config/ returns nothing. Two secondary effects worth checking during remediation, both marked medium confidence because neither was verified live: (1) with the customer base being US school districts, hundreds of students behind one NAT egress IP share a single bucket, so an IP-keyed limit is simultaneously too loose for an attacker and too tight for a legitimate 8am login surge; (2) Rack::Attack uses Rack::Request#ip, not Rails' RemoteIp middleware, so behind the GCLB the key may resolve to the proxy rather than the client -- which would collapse all traffic into one bucket. Both are testable with a request-header trace against a candidate revision. | adversary: confirmed -- Single throttle keyed on req.ip only; no lockout/failed_attempts counters anywhere in app/lib/config. Bonus: period_proc is a dead ternary (both branches return 3.seconds), so protected paths get no tighter window than general traffic.

findings.title: A Redis RDB persistence snapshot was tracked in git and shipped in every production container image for ~6 months; removed from HEAD (2026-08-14) but the blob remains fully retrievable from public git history at ced829ba1 on both staging and main

evidence.source: bash:git ls-files / git log / redis-server (isolated scratch instance, localhost-only) -- TTL-indifferent re-inspection 2026-08-16, correcting the 2026-08-14 pass
evidence.snippet: CORRECTED 2026-08-16 (see notes for why the 2026-08-14 result was invalid). The 2026-08-14 inspection loaded the file into a standalone redis-server and read DBSIZE=3 -- but a standalone (non-replica) Redis server silently discards already-expired keys while loading an RDB, and the file's own header (git cat-file -p origin/staging:dump.rdb, bytes 80-86: FE 00 FB 5A 31 5A 2E, RDB length-encoding decodes to SELECTDB 0 / RESIZEDB hash-size=6705 expires-size=6702) proves it held 6705 top-level keys, 6702 with an expiry. All 6702 were already past their TTL by August 2026 (file dated 2026-01-29/30) and were invisibly dropped before DBSIZE was ever read, so the 2026-08-14 conclusion never actually saw 99.96% of the file's keys -- including the exact TTL-bearing classes (/admin/auth/<token> at session_controller.rb:251, token_popout_*/token_tmp_*/oauth_*/saml_* at session_controller.rb:305-1230, all namespaced 'lingolinq-permissions:'/'lingolinq-stash:' via config/initializers/resque.rb:115-116, which shares one Redis connection with Resque) the original finding was actually worried about. Corrected method, TTL-indifferent: (1) loaded the blob into an isolated scratch redis-server (localhost-only, --replicaof pointed at an unreachable host so it never syncs, no persistence, torn down after) started WITH replica config, which does not evict expired keys on load -- DBSIZE=6705, matching the header exactly. (2) Independently and more importantly, ran `strings -n 6` across the full 774,639-byte raw blob (git cat-file -p, not a live load) -- this reads every byte regardless of TTL or Redis's read-time expiry filtering, and Redis key names are always stored as plain uncompressed strings (LZF compression only ever applies to individual string VALUES above ~20 bytes, never to key names), so this is a definitive, decompression-independent test for whether ANY key with a given name/prefix exists anywhere in the file, live or expired. Zero occurrences of 'lingolinq-permissions' or 'lingolinq-stash' (the two namespace prefixes EVERY admin-token/oauth/saml/token_popout/token_tmp key would carry) anywhere in the file. Zero occurrences of 'admin/auth', 'token_popout', 'token_tmp', 'oauth_', 'saml_' as literal substrings. Zero email-shaped strings, zero password/bearer-token/api_key/AWS-key(AKIA)/JWT-shaped strings anywhere in the byte stream. (3) Full key-name-pattern breakdown of the 6705 keys (via strings, normalized): 6615 'scheduled/WordData/<md5>' + 24 Board + 21 WeeklyStatsSummary + 21 ClusterLocation + 13 LogSession + 4 BoardDownstreamButtonSet + 2 Webhook + 1 User + 1 ButtonImage (6702 total, all under the 'lingolinq-development:scheduled/' prefix -- these are job-scheduling debounce/dedup markers, set with a TTL immediately before enqueueing a background job and checked before scheduling a duplicate, not session or credential material) plus the 3 non-expired keys already characterized on 2026-08-14 (2 Resque queue lists + the queue-name set, all domain::localhost:5000, dev-seed ids 1-19, job args numeric/global_id/boolean only). Conclusion holds, now on defensible evidence: no admin console token map, no token_popout/oauth/saml material, no session material, no PII, no secrets -- a stale local-dev Resque job-scheduling backlog only. This does NOT resolve the separate, still-open concern below: the blob remains retrievable from public git history regardless of file contents.

remediation.options: (1) DONE 2026-08-16 (corrected; see evidence): inspected the file's actual contents with a TTL-indifferent method -- confirmed clean, a stale local-dev Resque job-scheduling backlog, no rotation needed. (2) DONE 2026-08-14: git rm --cached dump.rdb; added *.rdb / dump.rdb to .gitignore and .dockerignore so it can no longer be committed or shipped in a container image going forward. (3) A .gitleaks.toml entry was considered and skipped: gitleaks does content-based secret scanning and can't meaningfully scan a binary RDB anyway; the .gitignore/.dockerignore change is the effective forward control. (4) DECIDED 2026-08-17 (Scot, risk accepted -- see notes): no git history rewrite. The blob remains fully retrievable from public git history at ced829ba1 (2026-01-30, ancestor of both origin/staging and origin/main; repo visibility is PUBLIC) via any clone, fork, or `git log -p`, and will stay there indefinitely -- this is a deliberate, informed decision, not an oversight. A history rewrite (filter-repo + coordinated force-push, breaking every existing clone/fork, and not even guaranteed complete given the repo's existing fork and GitHub's fork-network blob caching) was assessed as disruptive with no real security benefit given the confirmed-clean contents, and rejected on that basis.
remediation.timeframe: content inspection and forward-fix complete 2026-08-16; history-rewrite decision closed 2026-08-17 (risk accepted, not remediated)

closureEvidence.verifierNote: Residual, accepted 2026-08-17 (Scot), not remediated: dump.rdb (blob 4c38846c751ebed1ef1c8095aaa9682af47783d3) remains fully retrievable from public git history at commit ced829ba1 (2026-01-30), which is an ancestor of both origin/staging and origin/main in a PUBLIC GitHub repo (verified 2026-08-16 via `git merge-base --is-ancestor` and `gh repo view --json visibility`). git rm --cached only stops future commits from tracking it; it does not remove it from history. Inspected format only (not content secrets): a REDIS0010 snapshot with ~6,705 keys from a development environment (LogSession/Board/ButtonImage/Resque queue key patterns). | dual-review adversary (2026-08-14): flagged this finding's PUBLICATION (once merged/pushed) as a Critical in its own right -- a precise, indexed pointer to a still-present secret-bearing file in a public repo, independent of what the file actually contains. | remediation (2026-08-14, Scot-authorized), SUPERSEDED 2026-08-16 -- see below: content inspection was attempted via a standalone redis-server load (DBSIZE=3) and concluded 'no session material of any kind was present.' | CORRECTION (2026-08-16, independent second dual-review pass, adversary-caught + self-verified): the 2026-08-14 method was invalid. Severity remains 'high' and status remains 'remediated-unverified,' now with a populated closureEvidence.verifierNote naming the one residual this finding does NOT resolve -- the blob's continued retrievability from public git history -- since only Scot closes a finding, downgrades severity, or decides on the history-rewrite tradeoff. | DECISION (2026-08-17, Scot): ratified the recommendation not to rewrite git history, given the confirmed-clean contents and the real cost of a rewrite (force-push breaking every clone/fork, plus an existing fork and GitHub's fork-network caching mean it might not even fully remove the blob). This is Scot explicitly accepting the residual historical-exposure risk, not a reopened question -- the blob will remain in public git history at ced829ba1 indefinitely. Status/severity deliberately left unchanged (remediated-unverified / high) rather than moved to accepted-risk or closed: the ask was specifically to keep this visible in the register as a standing fact, not to formally close the record.

findings.title: The blocking secret-detection gate downloads and executes an unpinned, unverified gitleaks binary resolved at runtime from the GitHub releases API

remediation.options: Use the pinned version as the primary path rather than the fallback, and verify integrity before execution: keep GITLEAKS_VERSION as the source of truth, download only that asset, and check the archive against a committed SHA-256 (or verify the release signature) before extracting and running it. If tracking the latest release is a deliberate goal, do it with a scheduled bump PR that updates the pin and the checksum together, so the change is reviewed rather than silently applied on the next CI run. Pair with the top-level permissions block already tracked as LL-5ae3d7ca2c so the executed binary does not inherit a repo-default read-write GITHUB_TOKEN.

findings.notes: Surfaced by infra finder on 2026-08-12. ci.yml:255-270 sets GITLEAKS_VERSION=8.30.1 and builds a pinned URL, then queries the releases API and OVERWRITES that URL with whatever the latest release resolves to, falling back to the pin only if the API call fails. The pin is therefore decorative on the normal path: the version actually executed is whatever upstream published most recently, with no checksum or signature verification, inside a required status check, in a job that also holds the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN. A compromised upstream release, or a compromised asset name match, executes in CI. Overlaps in surface (not in control) with LL-5ae3d7ca2c, which covers the token scope of the same job; this finding is about the integrity of the artifact being executed. Positive note for the register: at this SHA the secret-detection job itself IS blocking (no continue-on-error, gitleaks runs --exit-code 1 with no || true), which appears to make part of LL-52ff2a9a79's description stale. | adversary: confirmed -- ci.yml:253-270 overwrites the pinned URL with the GitHub releases API result, no checksum verification. Confirmed secret-detection is a required branch-protection context on staging, so this runs inside a blocking gate.

findings.title: No scheduled reconciler detects Cloud Run configuration drift introduced outside the deploy workflow, the exact path that once silently disabled the Bedrock BAA account assertion

evidence.snippet: # Cloud Run console edit). That needs a scheduled reconciler, which is deliberately not in

remediation.options: Run scripts/gcp/assert-runtime-secrets.sh on a schedule (a cron workflow, or Cloud Scheduler invoking a job) against the currently-serving revision, not only as the last step of a deploy. It already takes --required and --required-literal and already reads back the live revision, so the reconciler is mostly a trigger away. Alert on failure to a channel someone watches, and consider adding an org policy or IAM condition that discourages hand-run gcloud run deploy against the production service so the CI path is the only one that materially changes it.
